title: Do Deterministic Verifiers Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Paired Shared‑Candidate Evaluation
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired experiment (autocand_A1_prereg_v1) that measured whether coupling a deterministic NetOps verifier+gate (generate→validate→repair, max 1 automated repair) to a single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) changes safety outcomes when the identical initial LLM candidate is observed with and without gating. Using shared_initial_candidate semantics, one sampled generation was reused for both arms per intent. We evaluated 200 deterministically selected paired intents in a sandboxed Batfish‑style validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). All 200 shared initial candidates passed validation in both baseline and guarded arms (contingency n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0). The preregistered paired estimand (guarded minus baseline unsafe‑proposal rate) = 0.0; exact two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired‑bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0,0.0] (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10000). No automated repairs were applied. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the confirmatory contrast tests only validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates; it does not measure guarded‑conditioned regeneration, prompt engineering, or multi‑sample/model variance. We present the preregistered design, implementation and execution accounting, artifact‑grounded interpretation of the null result, and concrete recommendations for follow‑up designs that avoid ceiling effects.

sections.introduction:
Generative language models are increasingly proposed to translate high‑level operator intent into device configurations and sequenced maintenance workflows. For operational adoption, outputs must avoid reachability, isolation, or policy violations when applied to live networks. Prior surveys and empirical reports emphasize that production trustworthiness depends heavily on surrounding system machinery—retrieval, deterministic validators, gating policies, and repair loops—rather than the model alone [1]–[3]. Architectures that combine generation with external deterministic validation and bounded repair (generate→validate→repair) are therefore widely advocated.

Research question. For a fixed intent→configuration task bank and one LLM, does coupling a deterministic validator and an accept/reject gate (with at most one automated repair attempt) to the identical sampled initial candidate reduce the incidence of unsafe proposals relative to observing that same candidate without gating? We formalized this as the preregistered estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline under shared_initial_candidate semantics.

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered paired design (autocand_A1_prereg_v1) that fixed generation semantics, sampling, model, validator, gate policy, repair budget, and analysis prior to observation; (2) an autonomous confirmatory run with gpt‑5‑mini and a Batfish‑style deterministic validator on n=200 deterministically selected paired intents under shared_initial_candidate semantics; (3) artifact‑grounded analysis showing complete concordance (every shared candidate valid) and no repair activity; (4) an evidence‑based interpretation of this degenerate null (ceiling effect); and (5) artifact‑supported recommendations for follow‑up preregistered designs that produce nondegenerate contrasts.
sections.related_work:
Recent literature has rapidly explored LLMs for NetOps and AIOps tasks including intent‑to‑configuration translation, runbook generation, RCA, and agentic automation proposals [1],[2]. Surveys and empirical studies document hallucination and unsafe‑command risks in operational contexts and argue for validator‑coupled pipelines, RAG anchoring, and external safety checks [1]–[3].

Empirical promise in adjacent domains. In adjacent domains such as program repair and DevOps automation, generate→validate→repair styles of architectures have shown promise under specific datasets and validators: for example, autonomous program‑repair agents that generate fixes and validate them against test suites have demonstrated measurable repair rates in controlled benchmarks [4]. Deterministic verification tools and distribution‑aware verification methods have also been used to detect or bound unsafe model outputs in other domains [5]. These works motivate validator‑coupled protocols for NetOps, but their reported gains are context‑dependent (dataset, validator coverage, and task abstraction) and do not by themselves establish universal safety guarantees for NetOps change execution.

Methodological gap. Two related evaluation gaps motivated our paired design. First, comparing pipelines while allowing different first‑pass model draws per arm conflates validator effects with model sampling variance. Second, many existing benchmarks emphasize QA/relevance or log/RCA metrics but lack tightly coupled intent→config items evaluated under deterministic validators with paired protocols that preserve initial candidate sampling. Our shared_initial_candidate experiment isolates the validator/gate effect on identical initial generations and therefore directly addresses the first gap.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration. We froze the primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline), generation semantics (shared_initial_candidate), model/adaptor (gpt‑5‑mini via hosted_netops_gvr_v1), deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and gate policy, repair budget (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1), task selection rule and sample size (task_count = 200 paired intents), and the analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1) before observing outputs (preregistration id: autocand_A1_prereg_v1).

Generation semantics and sampling. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics exactly one initial LLM generation was produced and deterministically reused for both baseline and guarded arms per paired intent. Because the same initial candidate is observed in both conditions, the paired estimand isolates only validator/repair/gate effects on that identical first‑pass candidate and does not measure any effect of guarded‑conditioned regeneration, prompt engineering, or model sampling variance.

Model and configuration. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json records declared_model_version="gpt-5-mini" and provider="openai_responses"). Adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementing Batfish‑style sequencing, precondition, group and minimum‑up constraints, and reachability/policy checks. The recorded model configuration includes max_output_tokens=2000, maximum_attempts_per_call=1, reasoning_effort="minimal", and temperature=null.

Temperature and sampling clarification (explicit). The run used temperature=null as recorded in the model configuration. Null or unset temperature in the recorded configuration is not evidence of deterministic model sampling (it does not imply temperature=0), and the adapter does not guarantee deterministic sampling; the executed design simply reused whatever single sampled generation the adapter returned per pair under shared_initial_candidate semantics and makes no claim of deterministic model draws.

Tasks, constraints, gating, and scoring. The deterministic task generator produced intent→configuration items with embedded constraints (allowed_fields, allowed_touched_fields, preserve_unspecified_state, workflow_policies, and explicit required_sequence). The preregistered sampler selected 200 paired intents using a deterministic index rule; selection was outcome‑independent. Baseline: observe the shared initial candidate without gating. Guarded: validate the identical shared candidate with deterministic_netops_validator_v5; upon violations, the deterministic gate allowed up to one automated repair attempt. Primary outcome: binary unsafe_flag = any reachability or workflow/policy violation after validator stabilization. Scoring used the rule full_intent_constraint_validation returning codes such as VALID_CONFIGURATION or explicit violation codes. Per‑episode validator traces and scoring outputs were archived and used for confirmatory scoring.

Confirmatory analysis. The primary confirmatory analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1. The 2×2 paired contingency compares unsafe_flag between baseline and guarded across pairs; the analysis reports discordant pair counts (n10, n01), an exact two‑sided McNemar‑equivalent p‑value, and a paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10,000). The preregistered missingness policy (complete_pair_primary) drops any pair with irrecoverable infrastructure failure; the run produced no such failures.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The run executed as preregistered: planned_episode_count = 400, completed_episode_count = 400, failed_episode_count = 0. Because shared_initial_candidate semantics requires one shared generation per pair, model_calls_used = 200 (one initial generation per pair). Provider audit showed 200 completed hosted model call events and no retriable provider failures. Deterministic reconciliation confirmed pair and episode accounting consistency.

Primary confirmatory outcome. The paired contingency table (guarded × baseline) was n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Every shared initial candidate was scored VALID_CONFIGURATION by deterministic_netops_validator_v5 in both arms. The paired estimate (guarded minus baseline unsafe‑proposal rate) = 0.0. The preregistered exact two‑sided test returned p = 1.0. The paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI is [0.0,0.0] with bootstrap_seed = 1729 and 10,000 resamples. The zero‑width CI arises from the absence of discordant pairs: every bootstrap resample of paired outcomes reproduces the same paired difference (0.0), producing zero empirical variance.

Repair and validator diagnostics. repair_applied = false for every guarded episode; no automated repair traces were recorded. Representative episodes demonstrate that parsed_command_count matched required_command_count and validator final_state satisfied the workflow sequencing and precondition checks for the recorded intents. The task bank exercised sequencing patterns (VLAN migrations, uplink failover, MTU changes) and group/minimum_up constraints in the validator's rule set.

Missingness and contamination. No pairs were excluded; complete_pairs = 200. The contamination summary recorded no flagged contamination items for the executed selection. Deterministic reconciliation asserted that all deterministic consistency checks passed.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded interpretation. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the confirmatory estimand isolates only validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates. Observing n11 = 200 implies that, for the chosen model (gpt‑5‑mini), the synthetic task bank, the prompt/template family, and the validator's ruleset, the sampled initial candidates satisfied the validator constraints; therefore the guarded machinery applied no repairs and changed no acceptance decisions. This degenerate null is an inferentially legitimate outcome supported directly by the archived contingency counts and validator traces.

Ceiling‑effect contributors. The artifacts point to three concrete contributors: (1) task‑bank alignment — the task generator encoded required_sequence and workflow_policies that match the prompt schema and validator checks, increasing the probability of syntactically correct outputs; (2) validator tightness and alignment — the deterministic validator covered the same sequencing and precondition checks used in task synthesis so correct syntactic mappings passed readily; and (3) shared_initial_candidate semantics — by reusing a single initial sample per pair the design removed model‑sampling variance that might otherwise produce discordant outcomes. Each of these contributors is traceable in the archived manifests and validator traces.

Design recommendations for nondegenerate inference. To detect verifier/gate value under realistic or adversarial regimes we recommend preregistered designs that intentionally avoid this ceiling effect: (a) increase baseline unsafe rates by augmenting the task bank with adversarial or out‑of‑distribution seeds; (b) use independent generation per condition (two independent model calls per pair) or multiple independent samples per condition to expose model sampling variance; (c) test multiple model variants or sampling temperatures to reveal variance and sensitivity; (d) increase the automated repair budget and allow iterative repair loops to assess repair effectiveness when initial violations are present; and (e) include human‑in‑the‑loop arms to evaluate operator decisions in response to validator flags. Each recommendation follows directly from the execution manifest and analysis artifacts and has straightforward implications for model_call budgeting and preregistered estimand specification.

Limits on interpretation. This null does not imply deterministic validators lack value in other regimes (e.g., adversarial inputs, independent per‑condition generation, or different models). Instead it demonstrates that design choices (task bank construction, generation semantics, validator rule coverage) determine whether a paired shared‑candidate contrast can detect verifier value. Field deployments require complementary evaluation regimes to quantify operational benefit and risk.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired experiment under shared_initial_candidate semantics comparing observation of a single LLM candidate (baseline) to deterministic validation and bounded repair of that same candidate (guarded). For the chosen configuration—gpt‑5‑mini, the supplied synthetic task bank, deterministic_netops_validator_v5, and shared_initial_candidate semantics—all 200 shared candidates were valid and no repairs were applied; the paired difference = 0.0 (p = 1.0) with a paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0,0.0]. This result is specific to the experimental design and does not contradict prior evidence that validators can reduce unsafe outputs under different regimes. We archive full artifacts and recommend follow‑up preregistered experiments that deliberately raise baseline unsafe rates or permit independent per‑condition generation to quantify verifier/gate contributions under more challenging conditions.

disclosure_statement: Preregistration and autonomy: this study was preregistered as autocand_A1_prereg_v1 and executed autonomously after the autonomy lock. Models and tools (concise): single LLM = gpt‑5‑mini (provider recorded as openai_responses); orchestration/adapter = hosted_netops_gvr_v1; deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; task generator = deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Human role and autonomy boundary: the human Research Director selected the topical family and constrained the initial prompt before the autonomy lock; literature review, preregistration, experiment execution, analysis, peer‑review emulation, and manuscript drafting occurred autonomously after the lock with no manual technical editing of manuscript content. Generation semantics clarification: executed and preregistered generation semantics were shared_initial_candidate (one sampled generation reused by both arms per pair); therefore the confirmatory estimand measures only validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates rather than effects from guarded‑conditioned regeneration or multiple independent model samples. Immutable master prompt locator and SHA‑256 (required): provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). The full execution and analysis artifact bundle is archived under the study record referenced by the preregistration id.
limitations: Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics mean baseline and guarded conditions began from an identical initial candidate; the confirmatory estimand therefore measures only validator/repair/gate effects on that same candidate and cannot assess effects of guarded‑conditioned regeneration or model sampling variance.

Construct validity: tasks were synthetic and deterministically selected; the binary unsafe_flag depends on validator coverage (reachability and workflow sequencing rules) and may not capture all operational risks (transient performance regressions or vendor‑specific side effects outside validator rules).

External validity: single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini), single deterministic validator, and synthetic intents limit generalizability to other models, validators, production topologies, or live device interactions.

Conclusion validity: the observed null effect (paired difference = 0) reflects this execution's sampling frame where baseline generation produced only valid candidates; the study was powered to detect approximately 10 percentage‑point reductions but cannot rule out smaller effects under different sampling or adversarial inputs.
Operational relevance: no live device changes were executed (sandboxed validation only); operational benefits (reduced triage time, deployment safety) were not measured.
Security/contamination: adversarial or poisoning scenarios were not exercised; no retrieval‑augmented generation was used, so retrieval‑based poisoning vectors were not evaluated.
Task‑bank reporting: per‑task difficulty labels and exact per‑label counts are available in the archived task manifest and should be consulted for detailed replay and follow‑up design decisions.
